subtopic: Euler Form, De Moivre's Theorem & Roots of a Complex Number
title: Worked: Euler form powers and 4th roots of unity

board_content.text: A power, and a full set of roots
Write $z=-1+i$ in Euler form and find $z^{8}$.
Now the four 4th roots of unity: $\alpha_k=e^{ik\pi/2}$, $k=0,1,2,3$.
Their sum is $1+i-1-i=0$, as the roots-of-unity theorem promises.
Four roots, not one — always $k=0$ to $n-1$.

segments_english.text: Let's exercise Euler form on a power, then list a complete set of roots.
Write z equals minus one plus i in Euler form, then find z to the eighth.
The modulus is root two, and the argument, being in quadrant two, is three pi over four. So z is root two times e to the i three pi over four.
Raise to the eighth: root two to the eighth is sixteen, and the angle becomes eight times three pi over four, which is six pi. e to the i six pi is one, so z to the eighth is just sixteen.
Now the four fourth roots of unity, using the roots-of-unity formula: alpha sub k equals e to the i k pi over two, for k zero, one, two, three.
Stepping k gives one, then i, then minus one, then minus i. A perfect square on the unit circle.
Their sum is one plus i minus one minus i, which is zero, exactly as the roots-of-unity theorem promises.
And note we listed four roots, not one. Always run k from zero to n minus one, and you'll never fall into the root-count trap.

segments_hinglish.text: Euler form ko ek power par exercise karte hain, phir ek complete set of roots list karte hain.
z equals minus one plus i ko Euler form mein likho, phir z to the eighth nikaalo.
Modulus hai root two, aur argument, quadrant two mein hone se, three pi over four. To z hai root two times e to the i three pi over four.
Eighth tak raise karo: root two to the eighth hai sixteen, aur angle ban jaata hai eight times three pi over four, jo hai six pi. e to the i six pi hai one, to z to the eighth bas sixteen hai.
Ab chaar fourth roots of unity, roots-of-unity formula se: alpha sub k barabar e to the i k pi over two, k zero, one, two, three ke liye.
k step karne se milta hai one, phir i, phir minus one, phir minus i. Unit circle par ek perfect square.
Unka sum hai one plus i minus one minus i, jo hai zero, bilkul jaisa roots-of-unity theorem promise karta hai.
Aur dhyaan do humne chaar roots list kiye, ek nahi. Hamesha k ko zero se n minus one tak chalao, aur aap kabhi root-count trap mein nahi giroge.
